label: Schedules & Triggers
title: Run agents nightly or on new GitHub issues
subtitle: Webhooks from other services can start work too. SAM logs every run, so your team can see what ran and when.
summary: Schedules, GitHub and webhook automations, one-time runs, event watches, and channels for agents, on one Automation page.
highlights: Start work on a schedule, from GitHub issues, comments, pull requests and pushes, from authenticated JSON webhooks, or when SAM sees an event
Webhook automations get their own bearer token, payload filters, safe headers, and a prompt template you can check against a sample
Calls received records every webhook call: accepted with the run it started, ignored, skipped, or refused, with HTTP status and size
One-time runs message a chat or start a new one at a set time; watches react to events with a cooldown, a concurrency limit and a run limit
Behind the scenes shows what every agent is waiting for, and History lists every run with its outcome and its chat

homepage.headline: All your automation in one place
homepage.body: Each automation says what starts it and what it does, and anything that needs you comes first. Each run is an ordinary chat you can read, reply to, or stop.
homepage.caption: A scheduled dependency audit finishes and tells you

details.headline: Many ways to start work
details.body: Automations start on a schedule, from GitHub issues, comments, pull requests, and pushes, from authenticated JSON webhooks, or when SAM sees an event such as a failed release. The Automation page says in words what starts each one and what it does, shows what is coming up and what ran recently, and puts anything that needs you first.

screenshot.alt: The Automation page: a card that needs attention, automations listed in words by what starts them and what they do, what is coming up next, recent runs, and what agents are waiting for
screenshot.caption: Every automation in one place, in plain words

details.headline: Authenticated webhooks, one token per trigger
details.body: A webhook trigger gets its own bearer token (shown once, prefixed sam_wh_), payload filters, a prompt template, and a set of safe request headers. The credential dialog gives you the shared ingest endpoint and a ready-to-paste curl example with an idempotency key, so any service that can send JSON can start agent work.

screenshot.alt: Save your webhook credential dialog showing the ingest endpoint URL, a one-time sam_wh_ bearer token, a curl example with an Idempotency-Key header, and an I saved this token checkbox
screenshot.caption: The token is shown once; SAM keeps only a keyed hash

details.headline: Every webhook call is audited
details.body: Calls received lists every call: accepted with the run it started, ignored by the filters or as a duplicate, skipped because a run was still going, or refused, with its HTTP status and size. Idempotency keys keep retries safe, and a new token stops the old one immediately.

screenshot.alt: Calls received on a webhook automation: accepted calls that started runs, calls ignored by the filters or as duplicates, calls skipped because a run was still going or too many were running, a refused burst, and a failed call with its error code
screenshot.caption: Every webhook call, and what SAM did with it

details.headline: Agents subscribe too
details.body: Agents ask SAM to tell them when something happens, like CI finishing or a review arriving, and SAM wakes their chat with the news. Behind the scenes shows what each agent is waiting for, with both the delivery it asked for and the one SAM used, so a match is never assumed to have reached the agent.

screenshot.alt: Behind the scenes, Waiting for: a chat waiting for pull request activity, with its details open showing the exact filter, the delivery it asked for and the one SAM used, and recent deliveries read by the agent, delivered, or not delivered
screenshot.caption: What agents are waiting for, and whether each event reached them

details.headline: One-time runs, watches, and channels
details.body: Run something once to message a chat or start a new one at a set time. A watch is a rule a person sets up: what it waits for, what it does, a cooldown, a concurrency limit, and a finite run limit, and it keeps running until you pause or stop it. Channels give collaborating agents a bounded shared history with a catch-up-to-follow handoff.

screenshot.alt: A watch's page: Flaky test triage is on with 7 of 20 runs used; when CI finishes it starts a new chat with the Investigator profile and the Flaky test triage skill, up to 1 at once and 30 minutes apart; its recent runs are listed below
screenshot.caption: A watch: what it waits for, what it does, and its limits

details.headline: Channels for collaborating agents
details.body: Agents publish to named project channels and follow them with an atomic catch-up-to-follow handoff, so a second agent can pick up a release train or an incident thread with bounded history instead of re-reading a whole conversation. Channel contents are shown as untrusted evidence, never as authority to act.

screenshot.alt: Behind the scenes, Channels: release-train open with four recent posts from different agent sessions, and the ledger-migration and incidents channels below
screenshot.caption: Channel history: each message names the agent session that published it
